disputed_date_policy: When credible sources conflict on a date, all competing dates are preserved in 'date_alternatives' with their sources. No single date is selected. The 'date' field gives the preferred or range form only when the conflict is immaterial or resolved.

events.claim: Quinn Chapel AME congregation formed (1844 as nondenominational prayer group; organized as AME 1847).
Olivet Baptist Church formed by merger of Zoar Baptist and Zion Baptist churches.
events.source: Wikipedia (Olivet Baptist Church) citing church histories

events.claim: Pekin Theatre opens at 2700 S. State (Robert T. Motts) — first Black-owned stock theater in the U.S. (opening year disputed: 1904 vs. June 18, 1905 first all-Black show).
Chicago Defender founded by Robert S. Abbott (May 5, 1905).
Binga Bank founded at 3633 S. State (Jesse Binga).
Anthony Overton moves to Chicago; Overton Hygienic relocated to Bronzeville.
Jack Johnson opens the Cafe de Champion on the Stroll.
NAACP adds its Chicago branch, among its first branches.
Wabash Avenue YMCA built (community fundraising + Julius Rosenwald philanthropy).
Dreamland Cafe opens (address disputed: 3520 vs. 3618 S. State).
events.source: UChicago Library exhibition text (1996-97); NPS nomination (1985)

events.claim: Oscar De Priest elected Chicago's first Black alderman (2nd Ward).
events.source: NPS National Register nomination (De Priest apartment building)

events.claim: Carter G. Woodson convenes the founding meeting of the ASNLH at the Wabash Avenue YMCA.
Monogram Theatre opens at 3436-3440 S. State.
Pilgrim Baptist Church founded out of the Union Grove Prayer Meeting Club. (congregation's claim; NMAAHC catalogs 1922)
red_team_notes: Cross-project audit harmonization 2026-09-28. H3: 1916 event qualified.

events.claim: Chicago Urban League founded; T. Arnold Hill first director.
Anthony Overton establishes Half-Century Magazine.
Metropolitan Theater opens (ca. 1917). Oscar De Priest establishes the People's Movement Club at Unity Hall (3140 S. Indiana).
The Olive Leaf Club (Bertie Boone and Maggie Walker) forms at 3732 S. Federal St.; becomes Liberty Baptist Church.
Royal Gardens ownership listed as Louis B. Anderson, William Bottoms, Virgil Williams (459 E. 31st).
Pekin Theatre reopens as a dance hall.
Vendome Theater opens (3143-3149 S. State). Frank L. Gillespie founds Liberty Life Insurance Company (later Supreme Life).
Chicago race riot (Red Summer); Binga's home bombed amid white resistance to Black residence outside the Black Belt (bombing count 5 vs. 6 — disputed).

Sunset Cafe opens August 3 (315-317 E. 35th). Royal Gardens becomes Lincoln Gardens (owner Florence Majors). Binga's private bank receives state charter as Binga State Bank. Supreme Life building built (Albert Anis).
events.source: Bo Lindstrom (2012); NPS nomination; Chicago Landmarks

events.claim: Overton commissions the Overton Hygienic Building (3619-27 S. State; architect Z. Erol Smith). Douglass National Bank opens (founding year disputed: 1921 vs. 1922 vs. 1923).
events.source: NPS nomination; Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (2019)

events.claim: Pilgrim Baptist purchases the former Kehilath Anshe Ma'ariv synagogue (3301 S. Indiana).
King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band at Lincoln Gardens.
Plantation Cafe opens (338 E. 35th). Supreme Life buys 3501 S. King Drive outright. Binga State Bank/Binga Arcade buildings (1924/1929). Lincoln Gardens fire, Christmas Eve.
Louis Armstrong with Erskine Tate at the Vendome Theater.
events.source: Bo Lindstrom (2012); UChicago Library exhibition text

events.claim: Anthony Overton founds the Chicago Bee (founding year disputed: 1925 vs. 1926).
Negro History Week organized at the Wabash YMCA (Feb 7) — origin of Black History Month. Apex Club era begins at 330 E. 35th. Savoy construction plans announced (Englestein syndicate).
events.source: Chicago History Museum (2023); Bo Lindstrom (2012); Jazz Age Chicago

events.claim: Savoy Ballroom opens November (4733 S. Parkway). Plantation Cafe bombed/burned (spring). Victory Monument erected at 35th & King Drive (8th Regiment). Overton receives NAACP Spingarn Medal. Racially restrictive covenant signed, Washington Park Subdivision, Woodlawn.
events.source: Jazz Age Chicago; Bo Lindstrom (2012); VT/Roanoke Times (1996); WikiLawSchool brief

events.claim: Regal Theater opens February 4 (4719-27 S. Parkway; $1.5M; National Theater Corp.). Oscar De Priest elected to Congress (seated April 15, 1929).
events.source: City of Chicago New Regal Theater report (1989); NPS nomination

events.claim: Chicago Bee Building commissioned; Binga opens the Arcade Building (35th & State); Supreme Life merger ($27M, reported). Ken Blewett starts at Regal as usher.
events.source: Chicago Literary Hall of Fame; BlackPast; City report

events.claim: James J. Gentry (Chicago Bee theater editor) coins 'Bronzeville'; the Bee sponsors an unsuccessful Mayor of Bronzeville contest.
date_alternatives: 1930 (Encyclopedia of Chicago: Gentry coined the word; Bee contest)

events.claim: Binga State Bank collapses (June).

National Theater Corp. sells the Regal to Balaban & Katz. Chicago Bee Building completed (3647-55 S. State). Ida B. Wells-Barnett dies. Gentry carries the 'Bronzeville' idea to the Defender's Robert Abbott; Charles Browning develops it into the Defender's 'second most profitable promotion'.
events.source: City of Chicago New Regal Theater report (1989); Encyclopedia of Chicago
red_team_notes: Cross-project audit harmonization 2026-09-28. H5: 1931 Gentry event downgraded with the coinage claim; origin is disputed.

events.claim: Douglass National Bank fails — the last Black bank in Chicago of the era. Sunset Cafe renamed New Sunset Cafe (October).
events.source: Academic article (National Negro Bankers Association); Bo Lindstrom (2012)

events.claim: Palm Tavern opens (446 E. 47th).
Burke v. Kleiman — Illinois class action upholds the Washington Park Subdivision covenant.
DuSable High School opens (February); Arthur Mitchell defeats De Priest for Congress (first Black Democrat in Congress, serves 1935-1943).
Carl Hansberry buys 6140 S. Rhodes; Anna M. Lee sues to enforce the covenant.
Ida B. Wells Homes constructed (PWA; dedicated Oct 27, 1940; first occupancy Jan 18, 1941). Ken Blewett becomes Regal manager — first Black B&K manager.
HOLC Residential Security map of Chicago: Black Belt/Bronzeville core graded D ('hazardous') — area D74 (35th-67th, State-Cottage Grove).

Hansberry v. Lee, 311 U.S. 32, decided: res judicata cannot bind inadequately represented class; covenant enforceability not reached on the merits. Exact decision day disputed (Nov 12, Nov 13, or Dec 12, 1940).
South Side Community Art Center founded (WPA Federal Art Project; dedicated by Eleanor Roosevelt 1941).
Mitchell v. United States decided for Mitchell (Jim Crow rail cars).
William L. Dawson elected to Congress (serves to 1970).
Drake & Cayton publish 'Black Metropolis' (Harcourt, Brace). Gwendolyn Brooks publishes 'A Street in Bronzeville'.
Overton dies (July 3); Chicago Bee folds 1947. Savoy Ballroom closes (year disputed: 1948 vs. 1954).
events.source: Clio; UChicago Library; Jazz Age Chicago

events.claim: Inception of the IIT/Mercy Hospital/Lake Meadows-Prairie Shores urban-renewal project — the city's largest at the time.
Shelley v. Kraemer renders restrictive covenants unenforceable; NY Life commits $18M to Lake Meadows; clearance of 100+ acres begins.

Vendome Theater demolished. Title I, Housing Act of 1949 (federal urban-renewal funding; $6.2M for the IIT/Mercy/Lake Meadows project). William L. Dawson becomes first African American to chair a standing House committee.
Douglas + Grand Boulevard population peaks at 193,302.
events.source: Rob Paral ('Chicago Community Areas Historical Data') via Wikipedia

events.claim: De Priest dies (May) at Provident Hospital. Gwendolyn Brooks wins the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry ('Annie Allen') — first African American Pulitzer winner. Jesse Binga dies (June 13).
Lake Meadows completed (~1,640 units; final 1,040 announced July 7, 1954).
Dan Ryan Expressway right-of-way clearance (1957-58); construction begins 1958.
Hansberry's 'A Raisin in the Sun' premieres (Bronzeville-family story).
First Dan Ryan segment opens (95th-71st), December 12, 1961; Clarence Darrow Homes built; S. B. Fuller buys the Regal from the Englestein Co. — first Black ownership.
Robert Taylor Homes opens March 5 (28 towers, 39th-54th, State St.). Prairie Shores erected (5 bldgs, 1,677 units). Dan Ryan fully opens December 15 ($300M).
Fuller loses the Regal (financial problems); the Regal closes (1968).
events.source: City of Chicago New Regal Theater report (1989)

events.claim: CTA Dan Ryan branch (Red Line) opens in the expressway median, September 28.
Madden Park Homes built — last CHA high-rise.
Metropolitan Theater demolished; Regal and Savoy demolished (1973).
Commission on Chicago Landmarks considers, then rejects, a Black Metropolis Historic District.
Six Black Metropolis properties individually listed on the NRHP April 30, 1986 (Thematic Resource multiple-property submission).
Eighth Regiment Armory renovation complete; reopens as the Chicago Military Academy (Bronzeville). ~$9M Wabash YMCA renovation by the Renaissance Collaborative.
Black Metropolis-Bronzeville District designated a Chicago Landmark (9 structures), September 9, 1998.
events.source: City of Chicago landmark address list

events.claim: Advocacy campaign: designate 8 Bronzeville structures as city landmarks (Roanoke Times); Chicago Bee Branch CPL opens; Sun-Times reports Supreme Life Building saved from demolition.
Michigan Boulevard Garden Apartments (Rosenwald Courts) closed by CHA.
CHA 'Plan for Transformation' launched (HOPE VI). Palm Tavern locked/closed.
Rosenwald Courts: Landmarks Illinois Most Endangered (2002); National Trust 11 Most Endangered (2003).
Ida B. Wells Homes (incl. Darrow, Madden Park) demolished 2002-11; Oakwood Shores redevelopment.
Quad Communities Development Corporation formed (LISC + Ald. Preckwinkle). Urban Juncture founded by Bernard Loyd.
Supreme Life Building rehab complete — Bronzeville Visitor Information Center opens.
Pilgrim Baptist Church gutted by fire (January 6); only walls remain.
Overton Hygienic Building $8M renovation (Davis Group) — spared from demolition. Robert Taylor Homes demolition complete (1998-2007; last tower 2007).
Rep. Bobby Rush introduces Black Metropolis National Heritage Area Study Act (never enacted); housing crash stalls Bronzeville redevelopment.
City buys Michael Reese Hospital site ($91M, Olympic bid); hospital demolished (Singer Pavilion remains).
Urban Juncture buys The Forum, saving it from demolition. Ida B. Wells Homes demolition complete.
WBEZ: Unity Hall 'in jeopardy,' vacant, most-endangered.
CPS closes 50 schools incl. Anthony Overton Elementary.
Shops and Lofts at 47 opens ($46M; Walmart anchor; 96 mixed-income units) — first Bronzeville mixed-use in 50+ years.
Washington Park Development Group buys Overton Elementary ($325,000, November 6).

Rosenwald Courts reopens as $132M mixed-use affordable housing. Sen. Durbin first introduces Bronzeville-Black Metropolis National Heritage Area Act. Anthony Overton Elementary listed on the NRHP (September 6).
Boxville opens (51st St. container marketplace). SSCAC named National Trust 'National Treasure.' Meyers Ace Hardware (Sunset Cafe building) closes. GRIT Chicago acquires Michael Reese site (June).
The Forum on Landmarks Illinois Most Endangered list. South Side Community Art Center listed on the NRHP (September 13). Chicago Bee Branch CPL reopens after $2.32M CHA-funded renovation (December).
events.source: Landmarks Illinois; NPS NRHP table; Citizen Newspaper Group (2018)

events.claim: The Forum listed on the NRHP (April 16). Victory Monument rededicated after $62K renovation (July 5).
August storm collapses Pilgrim Baptist's south wall.

Commission on Chicago Landmarks approves $200K+ Adopt-A-Landmark grant for Pilgrim Baptist stabilization (January). Bronzeville Lakefront approvals: Plan Commission (Feb), CDC $96.9M sale (May), City Council (July). 'The Light of Truth' Ida B. Wells National Monument unveiled (June 30). City Council backs The Forum rehab ($250K state grant, November). ~$2.1M state grant secured for National Museum of Gospel Music at Pilgrim Baptist site.
National Heritage Area Act passes Congress (December 2022); signed by President Biden January 5, 2023 (Public Law 117-339): Bronzeville-Black Metropolis National Heritage Area established.
Site prep begins at Bronzeville Lakefront (May).
City Bureau: Bronzeville home prices +~$200K (2018-22); gentrification debate feature (April).
Groundbreaking: BSCP Ladies Auxiliary Women's History Museum (Pullman Porter Museum expansion), March 29. Permits issued for SSCAC's $15M renovation (April), completion expected summer 2026.

Mayor proposes $5M Neighborhood Opportunity Fund grant for SSCAC expansion (April). Bronzeville Black Metropolis National Heritage Area + Renaissance Collaborative announce Wabash YMCA exhibition (February). Douglas + Grand Boulevard combined population 44,880 (2020 census, up from 40,167 in 2010).
events.source: chicago.gov (2026); EIN Presswire (2026); U.S. Census 2020 via Wikipedia

title: Bronzeville: Black Metropolis — The Rise, Fall, and Remaking of a Neighborhood
